item.title: PAL reconnects Saipan to Manila, Asia-Pacific destinations
item.description: Philippine Airlines will restore direct flights between Saipan and Manila on Oct. 26, re-establishing what the carrier calls an important air link between the CNMI, the Philippines, and major destinations across Asia ahead of the peak holiday travel season. In a media release, PAL said the reinstated route will give Saipan travelers “convenient and direct access to Manila,” with onward connections
item.content:encoded:
Philippine Airlines will restore direct flights between Saipan and Manila on Oct. 26, re-establishing what the carrier calls an important air link between the CNMI, the Philippines, and major destinations across Asia ahead of the peak holiday travel season.

In a media release, PAL said the reinstated route will give Saipan travelers “convenient and direct access to Manila,” with onward connections across its domestic network, including Cebu, Boracay, Bohol, Palawan, Iloilo and Davao.

The airline said the service will support a wide range of travel needs, from tourism and leisure to business, education, healthcare, and medical referrals, as well as visiting friends and relatives. It will also enhance Saipan’s access to PAL’s international network through Manila, with connections to Hong Kong, Bangkok, Singapore, Taipei, Tokyo, Osaka, Nagoya, Shanghai and Kuala Lumpur.

“This connectivity provides travelers from the CNMI with more convenient options for leisure and business travel across Asia and the Asia-Pacific region,” PAL said, adding that the route strengthens Manila’s role as a gateway between the Philippines and the Pacific.

The carrier said the restored service will also support travel to Saipan through a direct link from Manila, promoting tourism, business exchanges, and “stronger people-to-people ties between the Philippines and the Northern Mariana Islands.”

Passengers will receive PAL’s full-service experience, including inflight meals, baggage allowance, and “the warmth of Filipino hospitality throughout their journey.” Flights may be booked through PAL’s website, mobile app, hotline, ticket offices, and accredited travel agents.

Founded in 1941, PAL is Asia’s first commercial airline and operates nonstop flights from Manila and Cebu to 29 domestic and 40 international destinations. The carrier was recognized for the highest on-time performance among Asia-Pacific airlines in 2025 and was invited to join the oneworld Alliance in 2026.

item.title: Disturbance heading toward Marianas could develop into a tropical storm or typhoon
item.description: Forecasters are watching Invest 96W, a disturbance near Kosrae that could develop into a tropical storm or typhoon as it heads toward the Marianas. But the system’s track, timing and intensity are highly uncertain.
item.content:encoded:
Forecasters are watching Invest 96W, a disturbance near Kosrae that could develop into a tropical storm or typhoon as it heads toward the Marianas.

But the system’s track, timing and intensity are highly uncertain.

The system will continue to organize as it begins moving west-northwest toward the Marianas over the next few days, according to the National Weather Service.

It could pass anywhere from south of Guam to Alamagan in the far northern CNMI, likely sometime this upcoming weekend.

Forecasters are advising residents in the Marianas to maintain a general state of preparedness for the possibility of a passing tropical cyclone.

Meanwhile, Tropical Depression 28W with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph is expected to track to the northwest over the next few days, passing through the far northern CNMI near Agrihan as a tropical depression Tuesday night.

item.title: Shriners Children’s Hawaii returns to provide specialized care to Guam’s DPHSS patients
item.description: Shriners Children’s Hawaii and its Honolulu medical outreach team are returning to Guam Oct. 26-30 to provide free medical consultations for youth, according to the Department of Public Health and Social Services. The Honolulu medical outreach team will be providing free medical consultations for children up to 17 years old with orthopedic conditions, healed burns, or sports injuries at the Northe
item.content:encoded:
Shriners Children’s Hawaii and its Honolulu medical outreach team are returning to Guam Oct. 26-30 to provide free medical consultations for youth, according to the Department of Public Health and Social Services.

The Honolulu medical outreach team will be providing free medical consultations for children up to 17 years old with orthopedic conditions, healed burns, or sports injuries at the Northern Region Community Health Center in Dededo.

The Shriner's team was scheduled to assist in Guam in July, but the clinic was canceled due to Typhoon Bavi. Public Health is bringing the Honolulu team back to assist with the clinical backlog from the disaster.

For new patients, applications may be picked up at the Northern Region Community Health Center in Dededo, Room 30, Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 11 a.m. and from 1:30 p.m. to 4 p.m.

Parents and guardians may also request to receive the application by emailing DPHSS’s Medical Social Services staff, Cherisse Santiago at cherisse.santiago@dphss.guam.gov or Nicole Loren-Duplito at nicole.lored@dphss.guam.gov

Applicants must submit the completed application along with their child’s birth certificate, a parent identification card, and proof of legal guardianship, if applicable. A physician referral is not required, and Public Health says self-referrals are welcome.

For more information about upcoming on-island outreach clinics or to schedule a telehealth consultation, contact the Medical Social Services staff via email or call 671-634-7408.

item.title: New White House press secretary a 'devoted fan' of Trump and MAGA
item.description: President Trump's new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is expected to take the podium on Tuesday for her first press briefing. Zacharia steps in as Trump's chief spokesperson at a moment when his popularity has fallen to record lows and Republicans are scrambling to limit potential losses in the midterm elections. The Trump administration is also engaged in a legal battle with the press
item.content:encoded:
President Trump's new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is expected to take the podium on Tuesday for her first press briefing. Zacharia steps in as Trump's chief spokesperson at a moment when his popularity has fallen to record lows and Republicans are scrambling to limit potential losses in the midterm elections.

The Trump administration is also engaged in a legal battle with the press corps that work to cover Trump. Last month, the White House restricted access by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, news organizations that Trump views as unfriendly. The Justice Department has since launched an investigation into the five television networks that share pool video coverage of Trump.

In a post on social media, Zacharia , an attorney and a mother of four , offered no hint of the challenges ahead. She described her new job as the "honor of a lifetime" and praised Trump's policies. "His confidence is a true privilege, and his leadership is a blessing to this country," Zacharia wrote on Friday .

In naming Zacharia, Trump praised her longstanding personal loyalty . "She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," Trump said. "She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!"

Zacharia, 41, a graduate of Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, has worked for a number of conservative organizations, according to her online resume . She served on the advisory board for an anti-abortion group called The White Rose Resistance that took its name from Christian students who challenged the Nazis. White Rose says it's working to counter "the same evils, the same apathy " faced by opponents of the Nazi regime.

More recently, Zacharia has served as a communications advisor for the Trump Media & Technology Group, the firm that operates Trump's Truth Social platform. She has also been a frequent pro-Trump commentator on conservative outlets including Fox News and Newsmax.

During an appearance in August on the network Real America's Voice , Zacharia weighed in on the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, arguing that "toxic feminism" had skewed the public's view of the case. Clancy was charged with killing her three children. The 5-week trial ended in a mistrial after sparking a national conversation over postpartum depression.

"This started with the advocation of abortion," Zacharia said. "When women are championing the death and murder and the ability to murder their children from conception all the way through, when does humanity begin and end?"

Zacharia has also used her social media posts to amplify right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that Democratic leaders took part in pedophile rings. In one post from 2022, she described former Democratic White House chief of staff John Podesta as "Pedo Podesta." That same year she shared a post from a far-right commentator who claimed Democrats "want to mask and rape your children."

NPR asked the White House for comment on the posts, which were first uncovered by the online progressive media site , Popular Information. Administration officials responded in an email by praising Zacharia without addressing her social media comments.

After being named to serve as White House press secretary, Zacharia drew praise from other administration officials. FBI director Kash Patel described her as "sharp, fearless" and someone who "knows what it means to stand for the American people."

Karoline Leavitt, who held the press secretary post until August before stepping down, also praised Zacharia. "I have no doubt Katie will do great work for President Trump and our country," she said on X .

In an appearance on Fox News on Saturday , Zacharia boosted Trump's controversial plan to import Russian diesel fuel, which has drawn bipartisan criticism . She also praised Trump's efforts to rally GOP support ahead of the November vote, while suggesting congressional Republicans may be to blame for any losses.

"President Trump has made the case and delivered historic results. I would have loved to see more from our congressional Republicans and Senate," she said.

item.title: Government spent $10 million on pro-Trump ads after president said super PAC would fund
item.description: Ads promoting President Trump and his policies continued to be paid for by the U.S. government well after Trump announced he would have his MAGA Inc. super PAC take over funding the ads and kept airing despite a federal judge ordering them to come down. An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer dollars has been spent to air the ads since the campaign began in
item.content:encoded:
Ads promoting President Trump and his policies continued to be paid for by the U.S. government well after Trump announced he would have his MAGA Inc. super PAC take over funding the ads and kept airing despite a federal judge ordering them to come down.

An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer dollars has been spent to air the ads since the campaign began in late September. Nearly $10 million of that total was spent after Oct. 5, when the president pledged to fund it privately in a post on Truth Social .

"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump posted at the time. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc."

The ads have been criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle with Republicans praising the president's choice to shift funding for the ads to an outside super PAC. But, that praise was premature. Despite giving the impression that there'd been a policy change, the government-funded ads didn't stop airing after Trump's post.

The White House has repeatedly referred to the ads as public service announcements, but a lawsuit filed by Common Cause and others argued they were being funded without congressional approval and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda produced with taxpayer dollars.

The ads — five of them in all — cover a wide range of pro-Trump content. One includes a splashy montage of photos of the president with a chorus singing "love me" serving as the soundtrack. Another is an exact duplicate of an ad made by the Trump campaign during the 2024 election cycle. Two promote the military operations in Venezuela and Iran. All of them end with the words "Paid for by the U.S. Government" on the screen.

The spots continued being broadcast for several hours after a federal judge overseeing the lawsuit issued a temporary ruling Sunday night saying the government "shall cancel or cause to be cancelled any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged advertisements, including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026."

Pro-Trump spots aired hundreds of additional times Sunday night into the wee hours of Monday morning.

"The last PSAs paid for by the government aired yesterday evening," a White House official not authorized to speak publicly told NPR on Monday afternoon, adding that the government "did not receive notice from the court in time to cancel the ad buys. The PSAs will be paid for by outside groups moving forward."

The White House had previously said that taxpayer funds used for ads would not be reimbursed. The White House has also insisted these ads were merely about promoting patriotism. They argued the ads can't be campaign related because the president isn't running for office this year and have nothing to do with the midterm elections next month. But Trump has repeatedly implored voters to vote like he is on the ballot and his dismal approval ratings have been dragging down Republicans all over the country.

A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the ads are pretty unpopular. The poll asked whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to use "taxpayer funds to pay for election-related television ads featuring the President or members of his cabinet." It wasn't even close, with 86% of Americans saying it is inappropriate. Even 80% of Republicans said the ads were inappropriate.

It's rare to get such bipartisan agreement on anything these days.

item.content:encoded:
Actor Selma Blair was taken into custody after a flight from Los Angeles to New York for being physically abusive and injuring two flight attendants, authorities said Monday.

Police took Blair, 54, into custody late Sunday night when the Delta Air Lines plane was parked at the gate at New York's John F. Kennedy Airport, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said in a statement. There was no immediate response to a request for comment from the airline.

Blair and one of the flight attendants were taken to a hospital for evaluation, the Port Authority said.

The FBI, which is responsible for investigating all assaults aboard aircraft, declined to release details.

"Yesterday, we were informed by our partners at Port Authority Police Department of a potential assault aboard a flight that arrived into JFK. As per long-standing DOJ policy, we do not comment on ongoing investigations," said Sydney Kleinmann, a spokesman for the FBI NY.

Messages seeking comment were not immediately returned by the state and federal prosecutors' offices in New York.

A message left with Blair's publicist seeking comment was not immediately answered.

In a statement to several media outlets, a Blair representative said she had a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct.

Blair had major roles in films including 1999's "Cruel Intentions," 2001's "Legally Blonde" and 2004's "Hellboy."

In recent years she has been an advocate for disability rights. She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018. In 2023, she joined President Joe Biden at the White House to celebrate the anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act.

In 2016, Blair apologized for making statements she regretted on a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles, saying that she mixed alcohol with medication, which made her black out.

Associated Press journalist Michael R. Sisak contributed reporting.

item.title: Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's DC home, DOJ says it approved the warrant
item.description: Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., Monday morning. The Department of Justice said in a statement to NPR that agents with Homeland Security Investigations "executed a judicially authorized search warrant."
item.content:encoded:
Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., Monday morning.

The Department of Justice said in a statement to NPR that agents with Homeland Security Investigations "executed a judicially authorized search warrant."

The warrant was approved by the DOJ and is part of an "ongoing federal investigation." Federal authorities did not give further details on the reason for the probe.

Details about the investigation were confirmed by current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly.

One current official said this search is part of a multi-year probe that includes whistleblower complaints. A former official, who had previously been briefed on the matter, said the investigation deals with immigration fraud allegations.

Omar criticized the search on social media.

"Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Omar posted on social media. "I will not be silenced."

Several HSI agents could be seen walking near and around Omar's home on Monday.

Jackie Rogers, a spokesperson for the congresswoman, called the search an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

Sharon Jackson, 79, lives across the street from the congresswoman and said federal agents woke her up around 4:30 a.m. Monday morning.

"I got awakened by boom, boom, boom," Jackson said. "They were out here with a great big truck."

The search took place ahead of next month's midterm elections, in which Omar is seeking reelection.

Vice President Vance has previously alleged Omar committed immigration fraud — something she denies.
